candidate.title: Fake Online Pet Sale Scam
candidate.summary: Scammers post fake online or streetcorner ads for puppies and other pets at bargain prices, then demand upfront payment through untraceable methods before disappearing without ever delivering an animal.
safetyTips: Research the seller by searching their name or business online along with words like 'review,' 'scam,' or 'complaint'
Do a reverse image search on the pet's photo to check whether it has been copied from another site
Insist on an in-person or video visit with the actual animal before paying anything
Never pay with a gift card, wire transfer, payment app, or cryptocurrency for a pet purchase
Consider adopting from a local rescue or animal shelter instead of an online seller
Report suspected pet scams to the FTC at ReportFraud.ftc.gov
candidate.howItWorks: According to the FTC, scammers post ads (particularly for puppies) on social media, marketplace sites, or streetcorners, advertising purebred animals for a few hundred dollars when they normally cost thousands, and pressure buyers to act fast before the pet is "gone." The scammer relies on an appealing photo to draw the buyer in and insists on payment up front. Once payment is sent, the buyer never receives the pet, who may not even exist, and the money is gone. Some variations add extra "surprise" fees, such as claims that the animal is stuck at a shipping stopover and needs additional payment for permits or transport, which government agencies do not actually charge for domestic pet movement.
redFlags: Seller insists on payment before you can see or meet the pet in person or by video
Price seems far below what that breed normally costs and the seller pushes you to act fast
Payment is only accepted via gift card, payment app, cryptocurrency, or wire transfer service like Western Union or MoneyGram
Additional 'surprise' fees appear after payment, such as shipping, permits, or customs charges
The pet's photo turns up elsewhere online in a reverse image search, suggesting it was stolen from another listing
realExamples: FTC alert describing ads for purebred puppies priced at a few hundred dollars when they typically cost thousands, pressuring buyers to pay upfront before the puppy is sold to someone else

Pattern of sellers arranging pet transportation and then contacting buyers for repeated extra fees, claiming the animal is detained during a shipping stopover and needs a permit fee, as described by state animal health officials
candidate.source: FTC Consumer Advice, "Getting a pet? Avoid scams," https://consumer.ftc.gov/consumer-alerts/2024/12/getting-pet-avoid-scams

triage.reasoning: This is a specific pet-sale scam pattern not covered by existing generic titles like Fake Online Store Scam or Online Marketplace Buyer Scam, which focus on different mechanics (fake storefronts, buyer-side scams). However, the actual source text provided is FTC's general consumer alerts page and does not contain the specific pet scam details claimed in the candidate summary/how-it-works, so the claims cannot be verified against the given source text.
